questions.knowledge_point: Simplifying an Expression by Expanding Parentheses and Using the Pythagorean Identity
questions.worked_solution:
First, we expand the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta })+{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }+{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\cdot \frac{1}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }}+{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1+{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =1+({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =1+1 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that, in the last step, we simplified the right-hand side using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1.$ 

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta })+{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =2.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 1 \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

$$
2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -{cos}^{3}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .

$$
\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{3}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}
$$

Next, we use the Pythagorean identity to rewrite the expression in the parentheses, and then we simplify the resulting expression as much as possible.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot 1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we conclude that

$$
\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{3}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}=\operatorname{tan}⁡t.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Simplifying a Trigonometric Expression Using a Common Denominator and the Pythagorean Identity
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the first term using the definition of $\operatorname{tan}⁡x.$ This gives

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.
$$

Now, we put both terms over a common denominator, and combine the two fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x}-\frac{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x-{cos}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x-(\operatorname{cos}⁡x-{cos}^{2}⁡x)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify using the Pythagorean identity, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =\frac{({sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that:

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}=\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x}
$$

We put both terms over a common denominator, and combine the two fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{1}+\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t}{1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify using the Pythagorean identity, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}=\operatorname{sec}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡t(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t})=\operatorname{sec}⁡t.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We put both terms over a common denominator, and combine the two fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{1} \\  & \frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}{1(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)} \\  & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{({cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x=\frac{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Simplifying an Expression by Expanding Parentheses and Using the Pythagorean Identity
canonical_examples.problem: Simplify the expression $\sin x(2\cos x - \sin x) - \cos^2x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we expand the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x-{cos}^{2}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we group the $\sin^2 x$ and $\cos^2 x$ terms. 

$$
2\sin x\cos x -(\sin^2x + \cos^2 x)
$$

Then, we use $\sin^2{x} + \cos^2{x} = 1$ to simplify the expression in the parentheses:

$$
2\sin x\cos x - 1
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\sin x(2\cos x - \sin x) - \cos^2x = 2\sin x\cos x - 1.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Simplifying an Expression by Factoring and Using the Pythagorean Identity
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we factor $\sin^2\theta$ from the expression:

$$
\sin^4{\theta}+\sin^2{\theta}\cos^2{\theta} = \sin^2{\theta}\cdot(\sin^2{\theta}+\cos^2{\theta})
$$

Then, we use $\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1$ to simplify the expression in the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot ({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}) & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 1={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\sin^4{\theta}+\sin^2{\theta}\cos^2{\theta} = \sin^2\theta.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Simplifying a Rational Expression Using the Pythagorean Identity
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we factor the numerator:

$$
\dfrac {\cos \theta \sin^2 \theta + \cos^3 \theta} {\sin \theta}	=	\dfrac {\cos \theta \cdot (\sin^2 \theta + \cos^2 \theta)} {\sin \theta}
$$

Next, we use the Pythagorean identity to rewrite the expression in the parentheses, and then we simplify the resulting expression as much as possible.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot ({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (1)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that:

$$
\dfrac {\cos \theta \sin^2 \theta + \cos^3 \theta} {\sin \theta} = \cot \theta.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Simplifying a Trigonometric Expression Using a Common Denominator and the Pythagorean Identity
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the second term using the identity $\cot \theta = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta},$ as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\sin{\theta}}{1+\cos{\theta}}+\dfrac{\cos{\theta}}{\sin{\theta}}
$$

Next, we put both terms over a common denominator, and combine the two fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )} & = \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )} & \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )} & = \\ \frac{({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )} & = \\ \frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )} & = \\ \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } & = \\ \operatorname{csc}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\dfrac{\sin{\theta}}{1+\cos{\theta}}+\cot{\theta} = \csc\theta.
$$
